study_identification_part.si3_author_journal_year: Mariam Zabihi et al., Translational Psychiatry, 2020
study_identification_part.si4_title: Fractionating autism based on neuroanatomical normative modeling

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To introduce a novel methodological framework for parsing neuroanatomical subtypes within a large cohort of individuals with autism by combining normative modeling with clustering to summarize complex and highly individualized patterns of deviation into a small number of interpretable neurobiological subtypes, aiming to understand the heterogeneous neurobiology of autism.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Multi-class (one-vs-all) linear Support Vector Machine (SVM) for cluster separability and clinical separability; Spearman's correlation between atypicality index and ADOS-2, ADI-R, SRS-2, RBS-R, SSP, DSM-5 ADHD symptoms (inattention and hyper-impulsivity); Spearman's correlation between atypicality index and polygenic scores for seven traits (autism, ADHD, epilepsy, FIQ, neuroticism, schizophrenia, and cross disorder risk for psychiatric disorders); One-way ANOVAs with Tukey Honest Significant Differences for cluster differences in demographic and clinical measures; Chi-square statistic for sex distribution across clusters.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Five neuroanatomical subtypes of autism were identified based on cortical thickness deviations, which showed distinct morphometric differences and stronger associations with symptoms and polygenic risk within subtypes compared to the whole cohort.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Five putative neuroanatomical subtypes were identified based on cortical thickness (CT) deviations, with three showing widespread decreased CT and two showing increased CT. These subtypes were accurately classified out of sample, predicted differential symptom profiles, loaded differentially onto underlying genetic risk, and showed stronger associations with symptoms within subtypes than across the whole cohort. Specifically, cluster 1 was slightly younger and had more females, while cluster 2 showed higher impairment with lower IQ and more severe autism/ADHD symptoms. Cluster 3 was associated with core autism symptoms and polygenic risk for autism and schizophrenia, involving dorsal frontal eye fields, anterior cingulate, premotor, auditory, and temporal cortices. Cluster 2 was linked to comorbid ADHD symptoms and widespread cortical thinning in prefrontal, orbitofrontal, cingulate, somatosensory, parietal, and temporal regions. Cluster 4 showed cortical thickening in somatosensory, motor, parietal, associative visual cortex, and frontal eye fields, and was associated with inattention and hyper-impulsivity.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Large number of missing clinical and behavioral data; relatively low statistical power for genetic analysis; no manual edits on cortical surface reconstructions.
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: Firstly, there was a large number of missing clinical and behavioral data, which complicated analyses and led to a reduction of power in follow-up analyses. Most importantly, for the genetic analysis, the interpretation of the results should be made in the context of relatively low statistical power for each class and should be considered illustrative until our /uniFB01 ndings can be validated in larger cohorts. It is also possible that data were not missing at random. Secondly, regarding the anatomical data, we did not perform any manual edits on the cortical surface reconstructions.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study combines normative modeling with spectral clustering to identify neuroanatomical subtypes, capitalizing on both dimensional and categorical aspects of neurobiology, and uses 'atypicality index' (trimmed mean of top absolute deviations) to summarize individual deviations for clinical associations.
